plants-food.title: Plants make food
plants-food.sentence: Plants make their food from sunlight, air, and water.
plants-food.how: If a leaf gets no light, it cannot keep making food.
plants-food.extra: The green in a leaf catches the light.
quiz: What do plants use to make food?
What happens if a leaf gets no light?

plants-oxygen.title: Plants give off oxygen
plants-oxygen.sentence: In sunlight, plants give off oxygen.
plants-oxygen.how: People can collect the gas from water plants in bright light and test that it is oxygen.
plants-oxygen.extra: Plants also use some oxygen, but in bright sun they make more than they use.
quiz: What gas do plants give off in sunlight?
When do plants make more oxygen than they use?

bees-pollen.title: Bees carry pollen
bees-pollen.sentence: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower.
bees-pollen.how: You can watch yellow dust on a bee move from bloom to bloom.
quiz: What do bees carry between flowers?
Bees move pollen from flower to flower
Bees are a kind of metal

seeds-water.title: Seeds need water
seeds-water.sentence: Many seeds start to grow when they get water and warmth.
seeds-water.how: Give water to one seed and none to another, and you can see which one sprouts.
seeds-water.extra: Some seeds also need a cold spell first.
quiz: What helps many seeds start to grow?
How can you test what a seed needs?
Water one seed and leave another dry

fungi.title: Mushrooms are fungi
fungi.sentence: A mushroom is a fungus, not a plant.
fungi.how: Mushrooms do not make food from sunlight the way green plants do.
fungi.extra: Fungi get food from living or once-living things.
quiz: Why is a mushroom not a plant?
It does not make food from sunlight like a green plant

whales.title: Whales breathe air
whales.sentence: Whales are mammals, so they breathe air.
whales.how: Watchers see whales come up and blow out used air.
whales.extra: They cannot stay under the sea the way fish do.
quiz: Whales must come up to get

cactus.title: A cactus stores water
cactus.sentence: A cactus stores water in its stem.
cactus.how: Scientists measure water held in the thick stem.
cactus.extra: Spines help keep animals from eating that water.
quiz: Where does a cactus store water?
A cactus stores water in its stem
A cactus is a fossil bone

bird-bones.title: Light bird bones
bird-bones.sentence: Many bird bones are hollow, which helps birds stay light.
bird-bones.how: Scientists look inside bird bones and find air spaces.
quiz: Why are many bird bones hollow?
To help the bird stay light

coral.title: Coral is animals
coral.sentence: Coral reefs are built by tiny animals.
coral.how: Under a lens you can see the little coral animals in their cups.
coral.extra: The hard reef is made from their skeletons.
quiz: The hard part of a reef comes from

chimp-tools.title: Chimps use tools
chimp-tools.sentence: Some chimpanzees use sticks as tools.
chimp-tools.how: Jane Goodall watched a chimp peel a twig and use it to pull out insects.
chimp-tools.extra: She wrote down what she saw, day after day.
quiz: Who watched a chimp use a stick as a tool?
What did that chimp do with the stick?
Used it to pull out insects

dna.title: DNA is a ladder
dna.sentence: DNA is a long twisted ladder that holds instructions for a living thing.
dna.how: An X-ray picture and many later tests showed that twisted shape.
dna.extra: Rosalind Franklin took a key picture of DNA.
quiz: Who took a key X-ray picture of DNA?

evolution.title: Living things change
evolution.sentence: Living things change over a very long time.
evolution.how: Fossils, and the family trees of living things, are ways we test this idea.
evolution.extra: In science a theory is a big idea that has passed many tests.
quiz: Living things change over a very long time. That idea is
A wild guess with no tests
Which is one way we test that idea?

water-h2o.title: Water is H2O
water-h2o.sentence: Water is H2O, two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
water-h2o.how: When scientists split water, they get that same recipe every time.
water-h2o.extra: Ice is solid water, and it floats on liquid water.
quiz: How many hydrogen atoms are in one bit of water?

states.title: Three states
states.sentence: Matter can be a solid, a liquid, or a gas.
states.how: You can watch the same water be ice, then liquid, then steam.
states.extra: The tiny bits move more freely as it warms.
quiz: Ice, liquid water, and steam are
The same matter in three states
Which list names three states of matter?

ice-floats.title: Ice floats
ice-floats.how: Set a piece of ice in a glass of water and it stays at the top.
ice-floats.extra: Ice takes up more room than the same water as a liquid.
quiz: What does ice do in a glass of water?
It always sinks like a stone
It takes up more room than the same liquid water

water-boil.title: Water boils
water-boil.sentence: At sea level, water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
water-boil.how: A thermometer reads 100 degrees when the water is bubbling hard at sea level.
water-boil.extra: High on a mountain, water boils at a lower temperature.
quiz: At sea level, water boils at
On a high mountain, water boils

salt-dissolves.title: Salt dissolves
salt-dissolves.sentence: Salt can dissolve in water and seem to vanish.
salt-dissolves.how: The salt disappears from sight, but the water tastes salty, so the salt is still there.
salt-dissolves.extra: If the water dries up, the salt shows again.
quiz: How can dissolved salt show again?

rust.title: Iron rusts
rust.sentence: Iron rusts when it meets both water and air.
rust.how: A dry iron nail stays shiny longer than a wet one left in the air.
rust.extra: Rust is a new coat, not the shiny iron itself.
quiz: A dry nail kept from water
A nail left wet in the air
A nail with no test at all

glass-sand.title: Glass from sand
glass-sand.sentence: People make glass by heating sand with a few other minerals until it melts.
glass-sand.how: Glass shops melt the mix, then cool it into a clear solid.
glass-sand.extra: Some old windows are thicker at the bottom because of how the glass was made, not because glass drips.
quiz: Why is some old window glass thicker at the bottom?
Because of how it was made
Because glass slowly drips like honey

diamond-graphite.title: Carbon two ways
diamond-graphite.sentence: Diamond and pencil graphite are both carbon, packed in different ways.
diamond-graphite.how: Tests show both are carbon atoms locked in different patterns.
diamond-graphite.extra: That is why one is hard and clear and the other is soft and dark.
quiz: Diamond and pencil graphite are both
Why can carbon be hard or soft?
One of them is a planet
One of them is a theory

oil-floats.title: Oil floats
oil-floats.sentence: Oil floats on water because it is less dense.
oil-floats.how: Pour oil gently on water and the oil stays on top.
oil-floats.extra: A thin oil sheen can sit on a puddle for the same reason.
quiz: What does oil do on water?

plastic.title: Plastic chains
plastic.sentence: Most plastic is made of long chains of molecules, and a lot of it starts as oil.
plastic.how: Chemists link small molecules into long chains and then shape them.
plastic.extra: Some newer plastics are made from plants instead.
quiz: A lot of plastic starts as

gold.title: Gold does not rust
gold.sentence: Gold does not rust the way iron does.
gold.how: Old gold coins can stay shiny in air and water for a very long time.
gold.extra: Gold is still a metal, and it can be hammered very thin.
quiz: What does gold do in damp air?
It does not rust like iron
Gold can stay shiny for a very long time
Gold is a gas in the room
Gold is a kind of DNA

periodic.title: The element table
periodic.sentence: The periodic table lines the elements up by patterns in their atoms.
periodic.how: In that order, elements that act alike sit in families.
periodic.extra: Dmitri Mendeleev left gaps for elements people had not found yet.
quiz: What does the periodic table line up?
Who left gaps for elements not found yet?

force-push.title: A force is a push
force-push.sentence: A force is a push or a pull.
force-push.how: A spring scale stretches when you pull, and the stretch measures the force.
force-push.extra: Forces can start, stop, or turn a thing.
quiz: A spring scale measures a force because

magnet-poles.title: Two poles
magnet-poles.sentence: A magnet has two poles, called north and south.
magnet-poles.how: Hang a bar magnet so it can turn, and the same end keeps pointing north.
magnet-poles.extra: Every magnet we test has both poles, not just one.
quiz: How many poles does a magnet have?
The poles of a magnet are called

magnet-iron.title: Magnets pull iron
magnet-iron.sentence: A magnet pulls iron, but it does not pull wood, plastic, or copper.
magnet-iron.how: Test one magnet on an iron nail, a wooden stick, a plastic cup, and a copper coin.
quiz: Which one does a magnet pull?
Does a magnet pull every metal?

poles-push.title: Poles push or pull
poles-push.sentence: Opposite poles pull together, and the same poles push apart.
poles-push.how: Bring two magnet ends together and you can feel a pull or a push.
poles-push.extra: You cannot tell the poles by color. You tell them by how they act.
quiz: What do two north poles do?
What do a north pole and a south pole do?

gravity.title: Things fall
gravity.sentence: Dropped things fall toward Earth, and a theory of gravity explains that pull.
gravity.how: We measure falling things, weights, and the Moon path, and the theory predicts them well.
gravity.extra: Scientists still test gravity in new ways.
quiz: The deep idea of this pull is

sound-medium.title: Sound needs stuff
sound-medium.sentence: Sound needs something to travel through, so it cannot cross empty space.
sound-medium.how: A bell in a jar gets quieter as the air is pumped out.
sound-medium.extra: Sound moves faster in water than in air.

light-space.title: Light crosses space
light-space.sentence: Light can travel through empty space.
light-space.how: Sunlight reaches Earth across space, where there is almost no air.
light-space.extra: Drops of water can bend light into a rainbow.
quiz: What can bend light into a rainbow?
A dark closet with no light

friction.title: Friction slows slides
friction.sentence: Friction is a force that slows things that rub or slide.
friction.how: The same toy car rolls farther on a smooth floor than on rough carpet.
friction.extra: Friction also lets your shoes grip the ground.
quiz: Friction does what to sliding things?
A toy car rolls farther on

lever.title: A lever helps lift
lever.sentence: A lever can help you lift a heavy load with a smaller push.
lever.how: A stiff bar on a fulcrum lets you lift a book with less push.
quiz: Lift a heavy load with a smaller push
A seesaw is a kind of

inertia.title: Still stays still
inertia.sentence: A still object stays still until a force moves it.
inertia.how: A puck on smooth ice keeps going until a rub or a hit changes its motion.
inertia.extra: This rule is one of the motion rules Newton wrote.
quiz: A still book stays still until
Who wrote rules for how forces move things?

hot-air.title: Hot air rises
hot-air.sentence: Hot air rises above cooler air.
hot-air.how: Warm air from a heater climbs, while cooler air sinks.
hot-air.extra: That is why a room can feel warmer upstairs.

earth-sun.title: Earth goes around the Sun
earth-sun.sentence: The Earth goes around the Sun.
earth-sun.how: The way planets move, and pictures from space, fit a path around the Sun.
earth-sun.extra: Long ago people tested this against the idea that everything circled Earth.
quiz: Who wrote that Earth and the planets go around the Sun?

year-trip.title: A year is one trip
year-trip.sentence: A year is one trip of Earth around the Sun.
year-trip.how: We measure about 365 days from one season mark back to the same mark.
year-trip.extra: Some calendar years add a leap day so the count stays lined up.
quiz: One trip of Earth around the Sun
One spin of a toy top
About how many days is one Earth trip around the Sun?

day-spin.title: A day is a spin
day-spin.sentence: A day is about one full spin of Earth.
day-spin.how: The Sun seems to cross the sky once each time Earth turns.
day-spin.extra: Places take turns facing the Sun, which makes day and night.
quiz: Earth spins, so places take turns facing the Sun
The Sun goes out each night
The Moon covers the Sun every night

seasons.title: Why seasons happen
seasons.sentence: Seasons happen because Earth is tilted as it goes around the Sun.
seasons.how: The tilt changes how directly sunlight hits a place through the year.
seasons.extra: Seasons are not caused by Earth getting much closer to the Sun.
quiz: Earth getting much closer to the Sun
Earth's tilt changes how directly sunlight hits us
Summer happens because the Moon boils
Winter means Earth left the solar system
Seasons are a kind of metal

earth-layers.title: Earth has layers
earth-layers.sentence: Earth has a crust, a mantle, and a core.
earth-layers.how: Earthquake waves change speed inside Earth, which shows the layers.
earth-layers.extra: The crust is the thin outer layer we live on.
quiz: How do we know Earth has layers?
Earthquake waves change speed inside it

fossils.title: Fossils in rock
fossils.sentence: Fossils are remains or traces of living things kept in rock.
fossils.how: People find bones, shells, and footprints turned to stone in rock layers.
fossils.extra: Fossils are one way we know life has changed.
quiz: A bone or footprint kept in rock
Who found famous fossil sea animals in cliffs in England?

ocean-cover.title: Ocean covers most
ocean-cover.how: Maps and pictures from space show much more water than land.
ocean-cover.extra: About seven tenths of Earth's surface is ocean.
quiz: About how much of Earth's surface is ocean?

volcano.title: Volcanoes
volcano.sentence: A volcano can let melted rock come out of Earth.
volcano.how: People have watched lava flow out and then cool into rock.
volcano.extra: Not every mountain is a volcano.
quiz: What can come out of a volcano?

quake.title: Earthquakes
quake.sentence: An earthquake happens when rock under our feet slips.
quake.how: Instruments record the shaking, and cracks in the ground show where rock moved.
quake.extra: The shaking can travel a long way through rock.
quiz: What records the shaking of a quake?

soil.title: What soil is
soil.sentence: Soil is broken rock mixed with air, water, and bits of living things.
soil.how: A hand lens shows grains, roots, and dark bits of old plants.
soil.extra: Worms and tiny living things help mix soil.
quiz: Broken rock plus air, water, and bits of life
Who studied crops that help tired soil?

tides.title: The Moon and tides
tides.sentence: The Moon's pull helps make ocean tides.
tides.how: Tide times line up with where the Moon is in the sky, over and over.
tides.extra: The Sun's pull plays a part too.

weather-climate.title: Weather and climate
weather-climate.sentence: Weather is what the air does today, and climate is the pattern over many years.
weather-climate.how: One rainy day is weather, while records kept for years show the climate.
weather-climate.extra: A cold day does not erase a long warm pattern.

sun-star.title: The Sun is a star
sun-star.how: Its light and its makeup match other stars, only it is much closer.
sun-star.extra: Other stars look small because they are very far away.
quiz: Why do other stars look tiny?
They have no light at all

eight-planets.title: Eight planets
eight-planets.sentence: Eight planets go around the Sun.
eight-planets.how: Telescopes track eight big worlds on clear paths around the Sun.
eight-planets.extra: Pluto is called a dwarf planet, not one of the eight.
quiz: How many planets go around the Sun?

moon-light.title: The Moon reflects
moon-light.sentence: The Moon does not make its own light. It reflects the Sun.
moon-light.how: The bright part of the Moon always faces the Sun light.
moon-light.extra: The side in shadow looks dark.
quiz: The dark part of the Moon is

moon-phases.title: Moon phases
moon-phases.sentence: The Moon looks different each night because we see different amounts of its sunny side.
moon-phases.how: Draw the Moon for a month and the bright part grows and shrinks in order.
moon-phases.extra: A full loop of phases takes about one month.
quiz: Why does the Moon shape seem to change?
We see different amounts of its sunny side
A full loop of Moon phases takes about

saturn-rings.title: Saturn's rings
saturn-rings.sentence: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of ice and rock.
saturn-rings.how: Spacecraft and telescopes show vast crowds of chunks circling Saturn.
saturn-rings.extra: The rings are very wide, but they are also very thin.

milky-way.title: The Milky Way
milky-way.sentence: Our galaxy is called the Milky Way.
milky-way.how: We live inside it, and on a dark night its stars can look like a pale band.
milky-way.extra: A galaxy is a huge family of stars.
quiz: What is the name of our galaxy?

rockets.title: Rockets push gas
rockets.sentence: A rocket moves forward by pushing gas backward.
rockets.how: Let a balloon go and the air rushes out one way while the balloon zips the other way.
rockets.extra: The same kind of push sends real rockets up.
quiz: Pulling the stars with a rope
Air rushes out the other way

orbit-float.title: Floating in orbit
orbit-float.sentence: People in orbit float because they are falling around Earth, not because gravity is gone.
orbit-float.how: The ship and the people fall together, so they feel weightless inside.
orbit-float.extra: Gravity is still pulling. It bends their path around Earth.
quiz: Why do people in orbit float?

telescope.title: Telescopes gather light
telescope.sentence: A telescope gathers light so faint things look brighter.
telescope.how: A big lens or mirror collects more light than your eye alone.
telescope.extra: Galileo used a telescope to study the sky.
quiz: A telescope helps us see faint things because it
Who used a telescope and saw moons around Jupiter?

universe-stretch.title: Space may stretch
universe-stretch.sentence: Many far galaxies look redder, and a theory says space itself is stretching.
universe-stretch.how: That red shift lines up with distance for a huge number of galaxies.
universe-stretch.extra: This is a theory scientists keep testing, not a wild guess.
quiz: A theory about far galaxies says
The redder look of far galaxies is

life-beyond.title: Life beyond Earth
life-beyond.sentence: The idea that living things exist beyond Earth is a guess until a test shows them.
life-beyond.how: Spacecraft have checked some places, such as Mars, and have not found life there yet.
life-beyond.extra: A guess can become a fact only after a test shows it.
quiz: Have we found living things beyond Earth?
Yes, a city on the Sun
The idea of life beyond Earth is
A guess until a test shows it

heart.title: Your heart pumps
heart.sentence: Your heart pumps blood around your body.
heart.how: You can feel the beat as a pulse, and scans can watch the heart squeeze.
heart.extra: The beat gets faster after you run.
quiz: When does your heart usually beat faster?
When you are made of glass

lungs.title: Lungs and oxygen
lungs.sentence: Your lungs take in air so your blood can carry oxygen.
lungs.how: Tests show that blood picks up oxygen in the lungs.
quiz: Lungs help your blood pick up

bones.title: 206 bones
bones.sentence: A grown person's skeleton has 206 bones.
bones.how: Doctors count them on careful pictures and on skeletons in labs.
bones.extra: Babies have more bones, and some later join.
quiz: How many bones are in a grown person's skeleton?
More bones that later can join

muscles.title: Muscles pull
muscles.sentence: Muscles pull on bones. They do not push.
muscles.how: When your arm bends, a muscle gets shorter and pulls.
muscles.extra: Another muscle pulls the other way to straighten the arm.
quiz: Another muscle pulls the other way

germs.title: Germs and hands
germs.sentence: Some germs can cause illness, and washing hands with soap helps stop their spread.
germs.how: Tests show that soap and water lift germs off skin.
germs.extra: Soap and water work better than a quick rinse with water alone.
quiz: What helps stop germs spreading on hands?

senses.title: Five senses
senses.sentence: You can see, hear, smell, taste, and touch.
senses.how: Each of these senses uses its own body parts, such as eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and skin.
senses.extra: You also sense balance and heat.
quiz: Besides those five, you can also sense

enamel.title: Hard tooth coat
enamel.sentence: Teeth have a hard coat called enamel.
enamel.how: Dentists see enamel as the tough cover, and it is harder than the inside of the tooth.
enamel.extra: Sweet snacks and skipping the brush can hurt that coat.
quiz: The hard coat on a tooth is called
Harder than the inside of the tooth

brain.title: Your brain
brain.sentence: Your brain helps you think, feel, and move.
brain.how: Scans show parts of the brain working when you look, talk, or move.
brain.extra: You use many parts of your brain every day.
quiz: You use many parts of your brain every day
People use only a tiny speck and the rest is off
The brain is a bone in the foot
The brain is made of window glass

skin.title: Skin is biggest
skin.sentence: Skin is your body's biggest organ.
skin.how: Spread out, a grown person's skin covers more area than any other organ.
skin.extra: Skin helps keep water in and germs out.
quiz: Keep water in and germs out
Pump blood like a second heart

sleep.title: Sleep helps
sleep.sentence: Sleep helps you remember and gives your body time to grow.
sleep.how: Studies compare people after a full night of sleep and after too little sleep.
sleep.extra: Children need more sleep than grown-ups.

stomach.title: Stomach acid
stomach.sentence: Your stomach makes a strong acid that helps break down food.
stomach.how: Doctors can measure that acid, and food changes after it sits in the stomach.
stomach.extra: The stomach has a lining that stands up to its own acid.
quiz: Acid that helps break down food
Why does the stomach stand its own acid?
It is made only of diamond

helpful-germs.title: Some germs help
helpful-germs.sentence: Some germs help us, like the ones that turn milk into yogurt.
helpful-germs.how: People grow those germs on purpose, and the milk thickens into yogurt.
helpful-germs.extra: Many helpful germs live in soil too.
quiz: Only germs in space are real

mercury.title: Liquid metal
mercury.sentence: A metal can be a liquid at room temperature, and that metal is mercury.
mercury.how: In a sealed lab tube, mercury sits as a shiny liquid in an ordinary warm room.
mercury.extra: Mercury is poisonous. It is for looking, not for touching.
quiz: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
What should you do with mercury?
Leave it sealed and do not touch it

wood-frog.title: A frog can freeze
wood-frog.sentence: Some wood frogs can freeze in winter, then thaw and hop.
wood-frog.how: Scientists have watched these frogs freeze and later start moving again.
wood-frog.extra: Their bodies make a sugary liquid that helps protect their cells.
quiz: What can some wood frogs do?
What helps protect a wood frog's cells?

octopus-hearts.title: Three hearts
octopus-hearts.how: Studies of octopuses show two hearts by the gills and one for the rest of the body.
octopus-hearts.extra: When an octopus swims, the main heart can pause.
quiz: How many hearts does an octopus have?
Two of an octopus's hearts serve

banana-berry.title: A banana is a berry
banana-berry.sentence: A banana is a berry, and a strawberry is not.
banana-berry.how: Plant scientists sort fruits by how the flower parts grow, not by the grocery name.
quiz: Which one is a berry in science?

butterfly-feet.title: Taste with feet
butterfly-feet.how: Sensors on their feet find sweet plant juice, and then the tongue uncurls.
butterfly-feet.extra: The tongue is a long drinking tube.

wombat-cubes.title: Cube droppings
wombat-cubes.sentence: A wombat's droppings are cube shaped.
wombat-cubes.how: People have measured them, and studies of the intestine show how the cubes form.
wombat-cubes.extra: Cubes do not roll away as easily as round pellets.
quiz: What shape are a wombat's droppings?
Do not roll away as easily

sharks-trees.title: Sharks before trees
sharks-trees.sentence: Sharks were swimming before the first trees grew.
sharks-trees.how: Shark fossils in old rock sit below the first tree fossils.
sharks-trees.unsure: We are not sure of the exact years.
quiz: Trees, then the first sharks much later
Are we sure of the exact years for sharks and trees?

eiffel-heat.title: A tower grows
eiffel-heat.sentence: The Eiffel Tower stands a little taller on a hot day.
eiffel-heat.how: Iron expands when it heats, and measurements of the tower show a small gain.
eiffel-heat.extra: The change is a small stretch, not a whole extra floor.
quiz: On a hot day the Eiffel Tower
Why can the tower grow a little?
The Moon pulls the top off

lizard-tail.title: A new tail
lizard-tail.sentence: Some lizards can drop a tail and grow a new one.
lizard-tail.how: The tail can come off at a special spot, and a new one can grow.
lizard-tail.extra: The new tail is not exactly the same as the old one.
quiz: Drop a tail and grow a new one
Not exactly the same as the old one

venus-day.title: A long Venus day
venus-day.sentence: One full spin of Venus takes longer than its trip around the Sun.
venus-day.how: Radar measures the slow spin, and the orbit time is shorter.
venus-day.extra: Venus also spins backward compared with Earth.
quiz: How do we measure the slow spin of Venus?
With a magnet on a frog

darwin.when: Born 1809. His big book came out in 1859.
lines: Charles Darwin compared animals, plants, and fossils for many years.
In 1859 he published a theory. Living things that fit their homes tend to have more young, and groups change over a very long time.
Fossils are one way we test that theory.
darwin.extra: He spent years at home studying barnacles, one by one.
quiz: Who published a theory in 1859 about living things changing over a long time?

goodall.when: She began her chimp notes in 1960.
lines: Jane Goodall watched wild chimpanzees and wrote down what they really did.
In 1960 she saw a chimp use a stick to pull insects from a mound.
That record showed that chimps can make and use tools.
goodall.extra: In her notes the tool-using chimp was called David Greybeard.
quiz: Who saw a wild chimp use a stick as a tool?

carver.when: He did this crop work in the early 1900s.
lines: George Washington Carver studied crops and tired soil.
He showed farmers that peanuts and sweet potatoes could rest fields that had grown cotton for too long.
He also found new ways to use those plants so less was wasted.
quiz: Who used peanuts and sweet potatoes to help tired soil?

mcclintock.when: She studied corn for many years, and shared the jumping-gene idea in the 1950s.
lines: Barbara McClintock studied the colors of corn kernels.
She figured out that some bits of DNA can jump to a new place.
Later tests in other living things showed she was right.
mcclintock.extra: She learned it by looking closely, season after season.
quiz: Who found that some bits of DNA can jump?

just.when: He did his best-known cell work in the early 1900s.
lines: Ernest Everett Just studied the cells of sea animals.
He showed that the outer part of a cell helps control what the cell does.
He did that careful work at the shore and in the lab.
quiz: Who showed that the outside of a cell helps control the cell?

maathai.when: She studied living things, and the tree-planting work grew from the 1970s on.
lines: Wangari Maathai was a biologist who studied how trees, soil, and people fit together.
She led a movement that planted millions of trees.
Trees hold soil and help the air.
quiz: Who led people to plant millions of trees?

curie.when: Born 1867. She found polonium and radium in 1898.
lines: Marie Curie studied rays that some atoms give off.
She named that action radioactivity.
She found two elements, polonium and radium.
curie.extra: She named polonium after Poland, the land where she was born.
quiz: Who found the elements polonium and radium?

franklin.when: Her key DNA picture was made in 1952.
lines: Rosalind Franklin took careful X-ray pictures of DNA.
In 1952 one picture gave a clear clue that DNA is a twisted shape.
Other scientists used her picture when they built a model of DNA.
franklin.sceneAlt: A microscope on a bright table
quiz: Who took the 1952 X-ray picture that showed clues about the shape of DNA?

julian.when: His best-known chemistry work was in the 1930s and 1940s.
lines: Percy Julian was a chemist who built useful chemicals from plants.
He found ways to turn soybean chemicals into medicines.
One of those medicines was used to ease stiff joints.
quiz: Who made medicines from soybean chemicals?

tu.when: Her team drew the medicine out of the plant in the 1970s.
lines: Tu Youyou led a team that tested old plant cures.
In the 1970s they pulled a strong medicine, artemisinin, out of sweet wormwood.
That medicine helps people who have malaria.
tu.sceneAlt: Sweet wormwood, the plant artemisinin comes from
quiz: Who found artemisinin in sweet wormwood?

lines: Dmitri Mendeleev lined the elements up by their patterns.
In 1869 he left gaps where he thought missing elements should fit.
Later, people found elements that matched his gaps.
quiz: Who left gaps in the element table for elements not found yet?

lines: Alice Ball was a chemist who worked on oil from a tree seed.
In 1916 she found a way to change the oil so the body could take it in.
Her method made that medicine much easier to use.
quiz: Who found a way to turn a tree-seed oil into a medicine the body could take?

newton.when: His big book of motion and gravity came out in 1687.
lines: Isaac Newton wrote three rules that predict how things move when forces push them.
He also built a theory of gravity that covers both a falling apple and the Moon.
Scientists still test gravity in new ways.
newton.extra: He did think about falling apples and the Moon. We are not sure an apple hit him on the head.
quiz: Who wrote three rules for how forces move things?

faraday.when: He showed the magnet-and-current test in 1831.
lines: Michael Faraday found that a moving magnet can make an electric current.
That finding is how many generators make electricity.
He tested it with coils and magnets in the lab.
faraday.sceneAlt: A magnet pulling a piece of magnetite
quiz: Who found that a moving magnet can make an electric current?

wu.when: She ran the mirror test in 1956.
lines: Chien-Shiung Wu ran a very careful test on tiny particles.
She showed that they do not always act like their mirror image.
Her result changed a rule other physicists had trusted.
quiz: Who showed that tiny particles do not always match their mirror image?

lines: Ada Lovelace wrote about a planned calculating machine called the Analytical Engine.
In 1843 she published a step-by-step plan for the machine to compute numbers.
People call that plan the first computer program. The machine was not built in her lifetime.
quiz: Who wrote a step-by-step plan for a calculating machine in 1843?

jackson.when: She earned her physics doctorate in 1973.
lines: Shirley Ann Jackson is a physicist who studied tiny particles.
She researched how those particles behave, then how electrons move in special materials.
That work helped later studies of materials used in electronics.
quiz: Who studied tiny particles and how electrons move in materials?

ibn.when: He tested light about a thousand years ago.
lines: Hasan Ibn al-Haytham tested how light and seeing work.
He showed that we see because light enters the eye, not because the eye sends out beams.
He wrote the steps so someone else could try the tests.
ibn.unsure: We are not sure of the exact year he was born.
ibn.sceneAlt: A microscope on a bright table
quiz: Who showed that we see because light enters the eye?

anning.when: Her famous cliff finds were in the early 1800s.
lines: Mary Anning searched the cliffs at Lyme Regis for fossils.
In the early 1800s she found skeletons of ancient sea animals that were new to science.
Her finds helped people see that life long ago was different.
anning.sceneAlt: Lyme Regis, England, beside the sea cliffs
quiz: Who found fossil sea animals in the cliffs at Lyme Regis?

johnson.when: She checked spacecraft math in the 1960s.
lines: Katherine Johnson did the math for spacecraft paths.
Her numbers helped astronauts go up and come home.
Before one flight, astronauts asked for her to check the computer by hand.
quiz: Who checked the math for spacecraft paths?

jemison.when: She flew on a space shuttle in 1992.
lines: Mae Jemison trained as a doctor, then became an astronaut.
In 1992 she flew on a space shuttle and ran experiments in orbit.
The experiments looked at how bodies work away from Earth's usual pull.
jemison.extra: Before the flight she worked as a doctor.
jemison.sceneAlt: The Hubble Space Telescope above Earth
quiz: Who flew on a space shuttle in 1992 and ran experiments?

copernicus.when: His Sun-centered book came out in 1543.
lines: Nicolaus Copernicus wrote that Earth and the other planets go around the Sun.
His book came out in 1543.
A year is one of those trips around the Sun.
quiz: Whose 1543 book said Earth goes around the Sun?

lines: Galileo Galilei pointed a telescope at the sky.
In 1610 he saw four moons moving around Jupiter.
He also saw that Venus has phases, which fits a Sun-centered system.
galileo.sceneAlt: Jupiter's clouds, from NASA's Juno spacecraft
quiz: Who saw four moons around Jupiter in 1610?

chandra.when: He worked out the star limit in the 1930s.
lines: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar used math to study small faint stars called white dwarfs.
He found a weight limit. Past that limit, the star cannot hold itself up in the same way.
Later tests agreed with his theory.
chandra.sceneAlt: The Hubble Space Telescope above Earth
quiz: Who found a weight limit for white dwarf stars?

rain.title: Rainforest field station
lines: This station sits in the Amazon rainforest.
Scientists walk the forest and write down the plants and animals they find.
A field station is a work camp for watching living things up close.

lab.title: Chemistry lab
lines: Chemists work in labs inside buildings like this one.
Percy Julian did that kind of work with soybeans in the United States.
Careful measuring, and one change at a time, keeps a test fair.

sky.title: Observatory
lines: White telescope domes sit on a very tall mountain.
The air up there is thin and often above the clouds, so the sky looks darker and clearer.
Telescopes gather light from faint stars and galaxies.

cliff.title: Fossil cliff
lines: Layers of rock in these sea cliffs hold fossils.
Mary Anning found skeletons of ancient sea animals here in the early 1800s.
A fossil is a remain, or a trace, kept in rock.
cliff.alt: Lyme Regis, England, beside the sea cliffs

hospital.title: Hospital lab
lines: This is St Mary's Hospital in London.
In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed a mold that stopped germs in a dish.
That mold led to penicillin, a medicine that helps the body fight some illnesses.

ocean.title: The ocean
lines: Research ships leave the harbor and study the sea.
They measure water, map the bottom, and meet animals that live far from shore.
Most of Earth is ocean, so a ship is a moving lab.

stars.title: Star watchers
stars.sentence: People watched the stars and learned the patterns in the sky.
stars.more: Those patterns helped them track seasons.
stars.unsure: We are not sure who did this first.
stars.alt: Stonehenge, an old stone circle used to track the sky

microscopes.title: Microscopes
microscopes.sentence: Microscopes let people see tiny things no eye could see alone.
microscopes.more: A small lens bends light so a speck looks large.
microscopes.alt: A microscope on a bright table

germs.title: Germs
germs.sentence: Scientists tested the idea that some germs can cause illness.
germs.more: Louis Pasteur and others ran tests that supported germ theory. Washing hands still helps.
germs.alt: A lab dish with spots of germs

flight.title: Flight
flight.sentence: A powered airplane flew, and people could ride the air.
flight.more: The Wright brothers' plane lifted off in 1903.
flight.alt: A Wright Flyer replica hanging in a museum

dna.title: DNA
dna.sentence: Scientists showed that DNA is a twisted ladder.
dna.more: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray picture helped them see the shape.
dna.alt: A museum model of the DNA double helix

telescope.title: A space telescope
telescope.sentence: A telescope in space looked past the blur of Earth's air.
telescope.more: The Hubble Space Telescope launched in 1990. Newer space telescopes keep looking.
telescope.alt: The Hubble Space Telescope above Earth

p1-leaves.title: Sort the leaves
steps: Lay the leaves in a row.
Put them into two groups. You choose the rule.
Say the rule out loud. Big and small is fine. Smooth and rough is fine.
p1-leaves.done: You have two groups, and you can say how you sorted them.

p1-float.title: Sink or float
steps: Ask a grown-up to fill a bowl.
Guess sink or float for each object before you try it.
Lower one object at a time. Write what happened.
p1-float.done: The team has a list of what sank and what floated.

p2-shadow.title: Mark a shadow
steps: Stand a stick on flat ground in the sun.
Mark the tip of the shadow.
Come back later and mark it again. Say what changed.
p2-shadow.done: You have two marks and a sentence about the change.

p2-magnets.title: Magnet hunt
steps: Touch the magnet to each object.
Make two lists: sticks, and does not stick.
Circle the ones made of iron or steel.
p2-magnets.done: The team can point to something the magnet pulls and something it does not.

p3-sugar.title: Which water wins
steps: Ask a grown-up for warm water, not boiling water.
Put the same amount of sugar in each cup.
Stir both the same way. Watch which sugar vanishes first.
p3-sugar.done: You changed only the warmth, and you can say which cup was faster.

p3-ramp.title: How far does it roll
need: A tape measure or a string
steps: Let the car go from the top. Measure how far it rolls.
Do it three times the same way.
Then change one thing only, such as the ramp height, and try again.
p3-ramp.done: The team has two distances and can name the one thing they changed.

p4-celery.title: Watch water climb
steps: Ask a grown-up to color the water.
Stand the celery in the cup.
Look the next day. Where did the color go?
p4-celery.done: You can point to the path the colored water took.

p4-pulse.title: Count the beats
steps: Sit still. Count heartbeats for 30 seconds.
Jump for 30 seconds, then count again.
Write both numbers. Say what changed and what you kept the same.
p4-pulse.done: The team has two counts and a sentence about the difference.

p5-friction.title: Three surfaces
steps: Give the toy the same push on each surface.
See which slide goes farthest.
Name the force that slowed it. That force is friction.
p5-friction.done: You can rank the three surfaces and say why one was slower.

p5-drop.title: One change parachute
steps: Make two paper parachutes that match.
Drop them from the same height and time the fall.
Change one thing on one chute, such as the paper size. Test again.
p5-drop.done: The team can say which single change made the fall different.

p6-moon.title: Moon journal
need: A clear view of the sky
steps: Look for the Moon at the same time each night.
Draw the bright part. If clouds hide it, write clouds.
After a week, say how the bright part changed.
p6-moon.done: You have seven boxes and a sentence about the Moon's sunny side.

p6-planets.title: Planet order
steps: Put the Sun at one end.
Place eight planets in order from the Sun. Check a planet fact you have read.
Say one measured fact you used, and one thing that is still a theory.
p6-planets.done: The model is in order, and the team can name the fact they checked.

p7-ice.title: Which wrap keeps ice
steps: Leave one cube bare. Wrap one in paper. Wrap one in cloth.
Keep the room the same for all three.
Check every 5 minutes. Which cube lasts longest?
p7-ice.done: You changed only the wrap, and you can say what kept the ice longer.

p7-question.title: Your own fair test
need: A grown-up if you use water
steps: Pick a question you can test today.
Change one thing. Keep the rest the same. Measure the result.
Write what would change the result if you were careless.
p7-question.done: The team has a result, a unit, and one sentence about what would spoil the test.

print-fair.title: Fair test page
steps: Write the question.
Write the one thing you will change.
Write what you will keep the same, and what you will measure.
print-fair.done: Every box has a real answer, not a blank.

print-fact.title: Fact notes
steps: Copy one clear sentence.
Copy the how-we-know line.
Mark it: measured fact, theory, or guess.
print-fact.done: A reader can tell which kind of sentence you copied.

print-measure.title: Measure log
steps: Pick one thing to measure.
Measure it three times the same way.
Write the unit each time.

print-scientist.title: Scientist notes
steps: Write the scientist's name.
Write what they tested or figured out.
Write one question you still have.
print-scientist.done: The page is about their science, in your own short sentences.

time-stars: Are we sure who first watched the stars with care?
time-scope: What did microscopes in the 1600s let people see?
The center of Earth by eye
time-germs: Strong tests that germs can cause illness grew in which years?
Before Earth formed, and we are sure

time-dna: The twisted-ladder model of DNA was shown in
time-space: Why put a telescope in space?
To get above the blur of the air
